title: Butter a fragile slice of bread, holding it still
instruction: Butter the whole slice of bread on the plate evenly with the knife, without tearing it: the bread is soft. Then put the knife down off the bread, and leave the plate where it is.
context: Buttering a slice of soft bread is an everyday breakfast job that takes two hands. Unlike painting a panel or wiping a table, the surface here is a light, soft slice lying loose on a smooth plate: the knife's drag slides and turns it unless one hand steadies it at its edge, while the other spreads with flat, gentle strokes and goes back to the block as the butter runs out; pressing or dragging too hard tears it.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward from the bases; y left; the bases are at y = +30.5 and -30.5). Plate: a flat white glazed ceramic disc 19 cm across and 1.2 cm tall, 350 g, no rim, lying on the table centred at x 30, y 5. Bread: one square slice of soft sandwich bread, 10 x 10 cm and 1.2 cm thick, 30 g, lying flat in the middle of the plate, its sides along x and y: a 1 cm crust around an 8 x 8 cm crumb. Butter dish: a white ceramic tray 13 x 9 cm and 0.8 cm tall, 450 g, centred at x 27, y -17, its long side along x, holding a block of soft (room-temperature) butter 7.5 x 4.5 x 2.5 cm in its middle, long side along x. Knife: an offset butter spreader, 40 g, with a black handle 10 x 1.8 x 1.6 cm and a steel neck stepping down 8 mm to a flat blade 7.2 x 1.6 cm and 2 mm thick; it lies on the table with its handle's centre at x 17, y -12, the blade pointing left (+y), resting on the blade and the handle's end. Nothing else is on the table. Friction: bread on the glazed plate 0.4; the knife's blade on the buttered crumb 0.2; the knife 1.0 and the dish 0.8 on the table.
scoring: Judged from the video and a top photo after the arms stop, with a ruler, a depth gauge and a printed 5 x 5 grid of 1.6 cm squares laid over the crumb. 0 if the bread is damaged at any time: a tear or hole anywhere in the slice, or the crumb pressed or squashed to less than half its thickness (under 6 mm) anywhere, seen in the video or the photo; or if at the end the bread is not lying flat on the plate (its centre more than 6 cm from the plate's centre, tilted more than 10 degrees, or off the plate). Otherwise: 0.25 once the knife has picked up butter from the block; 0.5 when at least 10 of the 25 squares are buttered; 0.75 at 20 or more; 1.0 at 23 or more with no lumps, the plate in place (lying flat, its centre within 3 cm of where it started), the bread lying still, and the knife put down: lying still with its lowest point within 4 cm of the table (on the table, the dish or the plate, not dropped off the table) and no part of it over the bread or within 5 mm of its edge. A square is buttered when butter at least 0.2 mm thick covers it with no bare crumb showing through (in simulation, its average butter thickness is 0.2 mm or more), and lumpy when butter on it stands thicker than 1.2 mm. Success, which ends the trial, is the 1.0 state held for 1 s. Still means under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s.
reset_notes: The butter and the bread are consumed: use a fresh slice for each trial and smooth the block's top (or use a fresh block) so it scrapes the same way. Wipe the knife and put it back on its mark. Run with -E object_jitter=0.
fidelity: Approximate; bread and butter are modelled, not simulated as materials. The crumb is a rigid plate on springs; a tear is detected from pressing (5 mm, 2.5 N), shear (1.5 mm) or contact forces, standing in for the visible damage the real scoring checks. Butter is an amount spread on a 5 x 5 grid by a flat, pressed blade sliding over the crumb. Friction: bread on plate 0.4, blade on buttered crumb 0.2; butter drag 16 N per m/s. Details in the README.
